sources.news_title: Federal prosecutors accuse man of plotting attack on Mall of America
sources.text:
By Sarah Nelson and Jeff Day
The Minnesota Star Tribune
ST. PAUL, Minn. — A terrorism investigation has yielded an indictment against a Somali man from the Twin Cities accused of planning a mass casualty event at the Mall of America later this month, the Minnesota U.S. Attorney’s Office announced on Wednesday.
Federal authorities on Tuesday arrested Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, on one count of obtaining a firearm to carry out an act of terrorism. The indictment stems from a nearly two-year investigation that revealed Mohamud expressed intent to join and fight for terrorist organizations overseas but eventually turned to planning a terrorist-inspired attack in Minnesota when those plans failed.
| SPECIAL REPORT: Where is your agency losing time?
“Mohamud allegedly sought martyrdom in carrying out his plans to murder innocent civilians,” FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson said at a news conference Wednesday.
Mohamud was arrested on Tuesday by the FBI in a Richfield parking lot after purchasing an AK-47 rifle, four magazines and 200 rounds of ammunition for $600 from an undercover officer whom he thought was a member of ISIS.
He made his initial appearance on Wednesday afternoon in St. Paul federal court before Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright. He was appointed a federal defender and ordered to remain jailed ahead of an Oct. 19 detention hearing where a judge will determine his custody status ahead of trial.
U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said the charges “demonstrate that the threat of terrorism in support to ISIS and other foreign terrorist organizations is active and continuing.”
In a statement, the Mall of America said it “understands today’s news is unsettling and concerning for our guests, tenants, team members and the broader community.” The mall thanked the FBI and law enforcement partners for “their vigilance and extraordinary investigative work” in the case and added that it also maintains “multiple layers of security both visible and behind the scenes.”
The indictment largely focuses on Mohamud’s conversations with a person identified as a confidential source through various online platforms stretching back to December 2024. Mohamud frequently expressed his desire to travel and fight on behalf of the terrorist group on the platform, according to the charges.
“I wanna get martyred inshallah,” one of his messages said to a confidential informant.
“That’s why I wanna save up to go to another country or…get a gun here and just start killing a bunch of white ppl.”
In May of 2025, FBI agents attempted to interview Mohamud but his father told them he did not want to share “any information pertaining to himself or his son” with the FBI but would give their phone number to his attorney.
The terrorism charges come amid renewed concerns over gang violence in the Twin Cities between rival factions in the Somali community. Two recent shootings involving Somali teens as victims or suspects have left some in law enforcement calling for a regional task force to address gang activity while cautioning that the violence is stemming from a small number of people in the community.
One of the shootings at Eden Prairie High School’s homecoming football game forced the evacuation of athletes and fans. The other gang-related shooting in Bloomington resulted in more than 100 rounds fired along a residential street.
The indictment said Mohamud told the confidential source that he didn’t have enough money to travel to Somalia, and eventually started to discuss purchasing a firearm to carry out an attack at various locations in the Twin Cities, with a focus on the Mall of America “because it’s owned by jewish (sic) so if i kill even 30 people noone would go there anymore.” He also referenced carrying out a shooting at Valley Fair around Christmas time.
The indictment includes a screen shot of a message allegedly sent by Mohamud which says that “if i do an attack here im not doing it for any worldly matters im doing for the sake of Allah only.”
He then messaged, “don’t tell anyone this.”
Those plans turned into an agreement to purchase a firearm, the indictment said. By that point, Mohamud had pledged allegiance to ISIS through a selfie-style video, investigators said. Mohamud messaged the informant that he intended to carry out an attack on Oct. 24 during a festival at the Mall of America and sent a link to the Hmong Arts Celebration.
The indictment details how Mohamud allegedly pursued his attack, communicating over social media apps like TikTok, Telegram and Discord about whether to join the terrorist group Al-Shabaab or ISIS, he also showed growing exasperation with the direction of his life in America.
He wrote to the informant on Discord that he wasn’t doing well in school and, in March of this year, told the informant he planned to buy a “cheap BB gun” to train.
Mohamud wrote that his sister told him it was suspicious that he was planning to go to Africa and buying a fake gun. He told his sister that he had quit school and would be homeless in America in a few years since “houses and apartments are so expensive.”
The National Counterterrorism Innovation, Technology, and Education Center (NCITE) out of the University of Nebraska at Omaha keeps a database on federal charges for terrorism. Including Mohamud, 282 people have been charged for ISIS-related activity since 2014, when it was designated a foreign terrorist organization by the State Department.
Seamus Hughes, a senior research faculty at NCITE, said terrorism cases have leveled off in the last few years and are, typically, much more labor intensive for law enforcement. Suspects can be under 18, “which raises a whole host of issues,” and an informant is often needed because their overseas destination can oscillate.
He said the indictment against Mohamud “hits a lot of the normal trendlines we have seen in other cases.”
“A young man, terminally online, a lot of chat rooms, vacillates between wanting to travel overseas and join the fight to planning an attack here,” Hughes said.
The charges recall similar counterterrorism investigations from more than a decade ago when a wave of Somali-Americans from Minnesota faced charges for leaving the United States to fight alongside Islamic extremist groups. One major counterterrorism investigation in 2015 led to indictments against 11 Minnesotans charged in a conspiracy to provide material support to the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. Prior to those, the Justice Department brought similar terrorism charges following an investigation into the disappearance of up to 20 local men who left the Minneapolis area and traveled to Somalia to train or fight with terrorist group al-Shabaab.
The Justice Department is currently seeking to revoke the U.S. citizenship of one of the men who pleaded guilty to providing support to the terrorist organization al-Shabaab more than 20 years ago. The denaturalization case remains pending in federal court.

WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) – The FBI has arrested an 18-year-old man who had been plotting to carry out a mass shooting at the Mall of America near Minneapolis in the name of ISIS, according to court filings.
He was arrested on Tuesday after an FBI undercover agent sold the Minnesota man, Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, an AK-47, ammunition and magazines for $600, according to the complaint. Mohamud told the informant he planned to use the items to kill 30 to 60 people at an event at the mall in late October.
Mohamud was charged with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit an act of terrorism. His lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to the complaint, Mohamud told an FBI source on various messaging platforms that he intended to travel overseas to fight on behalf of al-Shabaab, a designated foreign terrorist organization. He said if he couldn’t travel, he planned to conduct a mass shooting. He later said he wanted to join ISIS.
He also allegedly expressed support for a man who rammed a truck into a crowd in New Orleans on January 1, 2025, killing 14, before being killed in a shootout with police.
In July, Mohamud allegedly said he wanted to kill 30 to 60 people at the Mall of America because he claimed its owners were Jewish, and he wanted to kill non-Muslims. He told the informant he planned an attack for October 24 because there was a “Hmong Arts Celebration” that day at the mall.
The Mall of America is the largest mall in the United States, with a theme park, an aquarium and more than 500 stores.
On Tuesday, Mohamud allegedly bought the AK-47, four 30-round-capacity magazines and about 200 rounds of ammunition from an FBI undercover agent. Soon after, FBI agents arrested him.
Mohamud made his initial court appearance before US Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright on Wednesday.

The Mall of America draws families from across the country. The Hmong Arts Celebration was supposed to be exactly what its name promised: a public celebration of art and culture.
According to prosecutors, Mohamud saw that crowd as an opportunity for mass murder.
The FBI saw the threat first.
Mohamud has been charged, not convicted. The allegations must still be proved in court, and he is presumed innocent unless and until a jury finds him guilty.

Minnesota teen charged in ISIS shooting plot at Mall of America
A Minnesota teenager has been arrested on allegations that he planned a mass shooting at the Mall of America in support of ISIS, according to federal prosecutors. He allegedly wanted to kill 30 to 60 people during an arts celebration later this month.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, of Richfield, was arrested on Tuesday after buying a disabled AK-47 rifle, four 30-round magazines and about 200 rounds of live ammunition from an undercover FBI employee, according to the criminal complaint. The planned target was the Mall of America in Bloomington, south of Minneapolis.
The suspect paid $600 cash during a recorded meeting inside the undercover employee’s vehicle near his home. He reaffirmed his plan to shoot people at the mall and was arrested at gunpoint shortly after leaving the vehicle with the weapon and ammunition. The FBI had rendered the rifle inoperable before the sale.
The investigation began in December 2024, when the suspect started exchanging hundreds of messages with a confidential FBI source through Telegram, Signal, Discord and TikTok. He discussed traveling to Somalia to join a terrorist organization and repeatedly said he would carry out an attack in Minnesota if he could not afford the trip.
The source, a paid FBI informant, posed as an ISIS member in Syria and later offered to connect the suspect with someone who sold guns, according to the complaint.
In July, the suspect said he did not have enough money to travel to Somalia and would instead attack in the United States. He initially discussed buying pistols and targeting the Mall of America or Valleyfair around Christmas.
He then focused on the mall because he claimed it was owned by Jews. In messages cited in the complaint, he said killing at least 30 people would stop others from going there and expressed a desire to emulate the Bondi Beach mass shooting in Australia.
In August, the suspect discussed recruiting someone from an online group of ISIS supporters to join the attack. He said he would carry out the shooting alone if no one could participate.
By September, he had selected October 24. “I can’t wait until I kill kuffar, man. October 24 is the day,” he wrote, using a derogatory term for non-Muslims.
Asked why he chose that date, the suspect said numerous Asians and other non-Muslims would be celebrating at the mall. He sent the source a link to a “Hmong Arts Celebration.”
The suspect also sent a video pledging allegiance to ISIS. A screenshot included in the complaint showed him with a red and white scarf covering his face and head.
Other messages expressed support for the 2025 New Year’s Day vehicle attack in New Orleans and a desire to imitate the Pulse nightclub shooting in Orlando, Florida.
When the source asked in September whether he was certain he wanted to proceed and told him he could back out, the suspect replied that he was “100% committed,” according to the complaint.
During Tuesday’s purchase, the suspect told the undercover employee that he planned to return home with the weapon when his mother was away. The employee had identified himself as an active ISIS member.
The suspect was charged on Wednesday with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition to commit a federal crime of terrorism, according to the Justice Department.

Mohamud responded that the date was “close,” according to investigators.
Two days later, he allegedly asked for a fully automatic firearm.

The weapon supplied during the sting was described in court records as a Norinco AK-47-style rifle, Model MAK-90 Sporter.
It came with four magazines and approximately 200 live rounds of ammunition.
The agreed price was $600.
Mohamud met the undercover operative Tuesday.
According to the complaint, he paid for the rifle and ammunition and left the undercover employee’s vehicle carrying the weapon.
FBI agents then moved in.

The underlying alleged terrorist conduct includes providing, attempting to provide, or conspiring to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.
Minnesota U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen announced the charge Wednesday alongside FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson.
The criminal complaint establishes allegations and probable cause; it does not constitute a conviction.
Mohamud is presumed innocent unless prosecutors prove the charge beyond a reasonable doubt.
It was not immediately clear Wednesday whether he had retained an attorney who could respond publicly to the government’s allegations.
Mall never attacked
The timing of the arrest is an important distinction in describing the case.
Federal authorities say Mohamud discussed attacking the Mall of America and took increasingly concrete steps toward obtaining a firearm.

That fact could become important if Mohamud’s defense eventually challenges the government’s investigation or raises questions about entrapment.

The government’s nearly two years of alleged messages with Mohamud are likely to become central evidence on that question.
Prosecutors contend those communications show Mohamud discussing violence and acquiring firearms long before the undercover agent offered him the AK-style rifle.

The alleged selection of the Mall of America carries particular significance because of the enormous number of people who pass through the complex.
The Bloomington mall says it receives more than 32 million visitors each year.
Its security department includes specialized units, extensive employee training, and multiple layers of emergency preparedness.
The property has faced terrorist threats before.
Al-Shabaab released a propaganda video in 2015 naming the Mall of America among Western shopping centers while encouraging attacks, prompting heightened security and warnings from federal officials.

More than a decade later, federal authorities say another person expressing support for foreign terrorist organizations was considering the same sprawling Minnesota landmark.
This time, investigators say they watched the alleged plan develop for nearly two years.
It ended Tuesday when Mohamud walked away from an undercover FBI employee carrying an AK-style rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition.

‘Chilling’ messages
Officials on Wednesday said Mohamud claimed to have joined ISIS a year ago and that they are charging him as a single actor.
“The messages this defendant allegedly sent to others were chilling,” said Christopher Dotson, special agent in charge at the FBI in Minneapolis.
Mohamud – who was born in the United States – will be held in custody until his detention hearing on October 19, according to court records. He made his initial appearance in court on Wednesday.

This July, Mohamud – who turned 18 in April – concluded he couldn’t afford to travel to Somalia, writing “so I will do the attack here,” according to the affidavit.

The FBI arrested him after he exited the vehicle.
A spokesperson from the Mall of America called the news “unsettling and concerning for our guests, tenants, team members and the broader community.”
“We are grateful to the FBI and its law enforcement partners for their vigilance and extraordinary investigative work in identifying, disrupting and removing this threat and protecting the community we all share,” they said. “We maintain multiple layers of security, both visible and behind the scenes, and will continue to work closely with local, state and federal law enforcement partners.”

Prosecutors detail scores of communications between Mohamud and the FBI source where he allegedly detailed his hopes of martyrdom, including one where he discussed just getting a "gun here and just start killing a bunch of white ppl."
By December 2025, Mohamud expressed interest in providing support to ISIS and the two regularly continued communicating as Mohamud shifted away from plans to travel overseas and instead indicated he was more intent on carrying out an attack in the U.S, the court documents allege. Throughout their communications, Mohamud allegedly suggested he had inspiration in his planned attacks from both the New Orleans New Years Eve attacker and Omar Mateen, the Pulse Nightclub shooter.
Prosecutors said Mohamud told the source he wanted to attack the Mall of America "because its owned by jewish" people, adding, "so if I kill even 30 people noone would go there anymore."
By August, Mohamud allegedly began planning a meetup with the source to purchase an AK-47 and ammunition, and Mohamud sent the following pictures of himself so the source could recognize him, prosecutors said.
Mohamud later allegedly settled on a meetup of Oct. 6 with the source to purchase the weapons and suggested he would plan to carry an attack on Oct. 24 targeting the Hmong Arts Celebration at the Mall of America, according to court documents.
During their meetup the undercover agent handed Mohamud a large duffel bag containing an AK-47 rifle and four magazines as well as a container with 200 rounds of ammunition, according to prosecutors.
The agent told Mohamud he was a member of ISIS and when he asked him about his attack plans, Mohamud again allegedly expressed intent to carry out a shooting at a festival at the Mall, and said part of his motivation was that he believed it was owned by Jews and that he was "angry at the bad treatment of Muslims" in the wake of the May attack on an Islamic Center in San Diego.
Upon exiting the vehicle, Mohamud was taken into custody at gunpoint by FBI agents, the affidavit says.
"The American people and the citizens of Minnesota should know from yesterday's arrest -- which was the culmination of an outstanding law enforcement and intelligence operation -- that federal law enforcement is standing up to their calling to protect us," U.S. attorney for Minnesota Dan Rosen said Wednesday. "Here, because of their vigilance and diligence, they were able to detect the threat and disrupt it before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, 'maybe 30 to 60 people,' as we allege in far greater detail in the complaint."
Rosen and FBI special agent Christopher Dodson detailed the extensive communications between Mohamud and an FBI confidential source that they said showed he was "100% committed" to carrying out an attack.
"The messages this defendant allegedly sent to others were chilling," Dodson said. "They show the idolization of ideologically motivated violence, a callous disregard for the sanctity of human life, a blind hatred of people of other faiths, and a cold commitment to carrying out his vision of violence in our community."
Mohamud is believed to be an American citizen born in the United States, Rosen told reporters, though in the criminal complaint he refers to Somalia as the homeland of his parents.
Rosen noted that in 2025 after being alerted to his sharing of extremist material online, the FBI actually went to Mohamud's house to attempt to speak to his parents but were rebuffed.
"I just would say to parents all over Minnesota -- for that matter, all over America: If you get the indication, especially if you hear from federal law enforcement that your son or daughter is being radicalized to the point where federal law law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded," Rosen said.

BLOOMINGTON, MN. (THECOUNT) — Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, has been arrested and federally charged after prosecutors say he was planning an ISIS-inspired mass shooting at the Mall of America targeting the Hmong Arts Celebration festival scheduled for October 24.
During an undercover FBI operation Tuesday, Mohamud allegedly purchased an AK-47-style rifle and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition from an undercover employee posing as an ISIS member, according to newly unsealed federal court records. Prosecutors say Mohamud intended to use the weapons in an attack that could have killed dozens of people.

The FBI began investigating Mohamud in December 2024 after a confidential source started communicating with him about either traveling overseas to fight for terrorist organizations or carrying out a mass-casualty attack in the United States, court documents allege.
Over the course of the investigation, prosecutors say Mohamud repeatedly discussed violence, martyrdom and his desire to kill people. In one exchange, he allegedly wrote about getting a gun and “start killing a bunch of white ppl.”
By December 2025, Mohamud was allegedly expressing interest in supporting ISIS. Investigators say his focus eventually shifted away from traveling overseas and toward carrying out an attack in Minnesota after he determined he did not have enough money to travel to Somalia.
According to the criminal complaint, Mohamud eventually identified the Mall of America as his preferred target. Prosecutors allege he told the confidential source he wanted to attack the shopping complex because he believed it was owned by Jewish people and said that killing approximately 30 people would discourage others from going there.
Mohamud also allegedly cited previous mass-casualty attacks as inspiration for his plans, including the New Orleans New Year’s Day attack and the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting in Orlando.
By August, prosecutors say Mohamud began arranging an in-person meeting with the confidential source to obtain a firearm and ammunition. He allegedly provided photographs of himself so the source could identify him and ultimately agreed to meet on October 6.
The alleged target date was October 24, when the Hmong Arts Celebration is scheduled to take place in the Mall of America’s Huntington Bank Rotunda. The event is scheduled for noon to 5 p.m.
During the October 6 meeting, the undercover FBI employee allegedly provided Mohamud with the rifle, four magazines and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition. Mohamud was taken into custody by FBI agents after leaving the vehicle, according to the affidavit.
U.S. Attorney for Minnesota Dan Rosen said Wednesday that the investigation disrupted the alleged plan before anyone was harmed.
“The American people and the citizens of Minnesota should know from yesterday’s arrest” that federal authorities detected and disrupted the threat, Rosen said, citing Mohamud’s alleged statement that he intended to kill “maybe 30 to 60 people.”
FBI Minneapolis Field Office Special Agent in Charge Christopher D. Dotson said the messages investigators obtained allegedly demonstrated Mohamud’s commitment to ideologically motivated violence and hatred toward people of other faiths.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American citizen born in the United States and that his parents are from Somalia.
Rosen also said the FBI had previously attempted to intervene after investigators became aware of extremist material Mohamud was allegedly sharing online. In 2025, agents went to Mohamud’s home in an attempt to speak with his parents, but they declined to meet with investigators.
Mohamud faces one federal count alleging that he knowingly received a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reason to believe they would be used to commit a federal crime of terrorism. The allegations remain unproven, and Mohamud is presumed innocent unless convicted in court.
The nearly two-year investigation ended without the planned attack taking place, and no one was injured during the operation.
The Mall of America is located in Bloomington in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metropolitan area, while Mohamud was arrested in nearby Richfield, Minnesota.
